Meanderings & Digressions · Data stories · November 2026

Reading for Fun Again

Three years of trading the television for a book

As a kid I read constantly, for no better reason than wanting to know what happened next. Somewhere along the way that stopped. Everything I read was for school or for work, and reading turned into homework. In the evenings I turned on the TV instead.

So I decided I wanted to read for fun again, and to spend less of my evenings looking at a screen. The list I keep of what I finish starts in 2024.It is a notes file, not a sophisticated system: 54 books by 18 authors, from January 2024 to 3 November 2026. It has no dates or ratings, only titles under a year. I looked up the page counts afterwards, and they vary a little by edition. I wanted to see what coming back to reading looks like.

Three shelves

Every book I finished, one spine each, as thick as its page count, shelved by year. Books by the same author stand together, largest group first, and a small gap separates one series from the next. Peter Heller is in orange. The dashed spine is the book I’m reading now.It looks like a habit coming back: 10 books in 2024, 19 in 2025, and 25 so far this year, which works out to a book every 12 days.

In pages the change is bigger: 3,965, then 11,252, then 12,101 with the year not over. That is 11 pages a day in 2024 and 39 a day now. These days I rarely turn on the TV during the week. I relax with a book instead.

The count is only half of it. Look at 2025. I nearly doubled my books that year and nearly tripled my pages, and I did it with 4 authors. Sarah J. Maas alone accounts for ten spines and 6,968 pages, 26 percent of everything on these shelves.

I didn’t quit bingeing, I moved it

Oddly though, I never gave up the habit television taught me. I took it with me. 39 of the 54 books, 72 percent, were read as part of a run.A run is two or more books from the same series in the same year. The longest is eight straight books of Dungeon Crawler Carl.

A series does for a reader what a season does for a viewer. When one book ends the next is already waiting, and there is nothing to decide on a Tuesday night.

These 9 authors are half of everyone on the list, and they wrote 45 of the 54 books. The other 9 authors got one book each.

One row is different. Every other name belongs to a single year, or two at most. Peter Heller is there in all three, never more than two books at a time. My guess is that it’s because his novels mostly stand alone. There is nothing to binge, so I keep coming back.

Nothing assigned

Fantasy and science fiction have been the base every year: 6 of 10, then 18 of 19, then 14 of 25. This year 7 thrillers joined them, all Jack Carr and Brad Thor, along with a Japanese murder mystery from the 1940s.

Nonfiction makes up 3 of the 54 books, and I don’t think that’s an accident. Nonfiction was what reading had turned into. To enjoy reading again, I had to stop reading anything useful for a while.

Almost everything is new

There is no syllabus here either. Half of what I read was published in 2019 or later, and 93 percent of it since 2012. The typical book was 6 years old when I got to it.

Two dots sit by themselves on the left: The Honjin Murders, from 1946, and A Wizard of Earthsea, from 1968. Both arrived this year.

What comes next

The habit is back, so the goal now is to mix in more nonfiction. Not as homework this time.

I’m currently reading Regenesis, George Church’s book on synthetic biology. It’s the dashed spine at the end of this year’s shelf.

As a kid I read to find out what happened next. It turns out that still works.

Data from my reading list, last updated 3 November 2026. Page counts and publication years are not in the list; they come from Open Library and publisher listings, and vary by edition. Charts are hand-built SVG; the data and the script that draws them are in Data/books.
